article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: Use immersive VR simulation as a safe complement to in-vivo classroom practice for training classroom management coping strategies
description: The article recommends VR simulation as a complement to traditional CRM teaching when real classroom time is insufficient or when realism conflicts with stimulus control and feedback. The 3B platform "aims to better prepare trainee teachers for future in vivo training by letting them experience and practice their coping strategies in a safe environment". Because real classroom disturbances are unpredictable, systematic CRM training currently relies on theory, video analysis, and role-play; an immersive simulation adds realistic stress exposure with controlled, repeatable stimuli and targeted real-time feedback.
requirements: The simulation must realistically elicit stress similar to a real classroom atmosphere, since stress exposure training rests on eliciting emotional responses
constraints: Consumer hardware cannot provide truly interactive photo-realism, so a balance between realism and overall performance (latency, frame rate) must be found
target_learners: Novice and trainee teachers who do not feel sufficiently prepared with regard to CRM
target_learning_goals: Establishing and maintaining order, engaging students, and developing coping strategies for disruptive behavior
examples: 3B was designed with CRM training experts who created the scenarios and virtual student behaviors, and underwent a one-year iterative user-centered development process
key_sources: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026

article_title: Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors
citation: Ke, F., Dai, Z., Pachman, M. et al. (2021). Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors. Instr Sci, 49, 831–854. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09555-4
title: Use VR-based teaching simulation to supplement or substitute for live classroom simulation in hosting participatory teaching development
description: The article recommends VR-based simulation as a complement or alternative to live classroom simulation for participatory training of student instructors. The authors state that "VR-based simulation can supplement and work as an alternative to the live classroom simulation to host participatory teaching development." The recommendation is qualified by the domain-specific knowledge results and the engagement limitation.
requirements: The VR simulation must provide domain-specific challenges and authentic environmental prompting to foster experiential and vicarious learning of teaching.
constraints: VR participants lacked mutual engagement in collaborative role-playing, so the format does not replicate the collaborative engagement of live simulation.
examples: 40 university teaching assistants completed a 4-h training session randomly assigned to a VR simulation or a live classroom simulation condition.
key_sources: Ke, F., Dai, Z., Pachman, M. et al. (2021). Exploring multiuser virtual teaching simulation as an alternative learning environment for student instructors. Instr Sci, 49, 831–854. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09555-4

article_title: Embodied word learning in schools and sustained attention in virtual reality
citation: Rudling, M., Rumetshofer, T., Nirme, J. & Mårtensson, J. (2026). Embodied Word Learning in Schools and Sustained Attention in Virtual Reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00395-2
title: VR object-assembly word-learning game and matched PC passive-viewing condition
description: The authors developed both training programs for this study: a VR game on Meta Quest Pro headsets, implemented in Unity 3D, in which children assembled 3D segmented ancient farming tools with hand controllers, after which the word appeared on a blackboard with a spoken recording played three times; and a matched PC condition in PsychoPy showing 15-second assembly videos without hands. The VR environment "was deliberately designed to minimize visual distractions". Each 18-word VR set took on average 19.40 minutes; each PC session took 8 minutes.
requirements: Head-mounted displays with hand controllers and inside-out movement tracking, and laptop delivery of the PC and recall tests
constraints: In this implementation the VR environment "is still richer than the very plain PC user interface", which the authors suggest may have added strain on attentional load
Words were exposed only once per learning phase and training lasted one week per condition
target_learning_goals: recognition and recall of 108 novel spoken and written word forms paired with unfamiliar objects
examples: Children assembled segmented objects from three to five pieces in VR, with pieces signalling correct connections by turning from white to green
In the PC condition children watched silent videos of objects assembling themselves from the same parts, then saw the word above a still image

article_title: Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality
citation: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6
title: Interactive VR salesperson paradigm for studying event segmentation of episodic memory
description: A custom-built VR environment (Unreal Engine 4.26, HTC Vive Pro 2) in which participants "acted as salespersons interacting with customers across different booths", delivering objects while remembering the order in which objects appeared. Mission boundaries were defined by customer identity and spatial boundaries by distinct booths, yielding a 2 x 2 design of within/across boundary conditions. Memory was assessed afterwards with a recency discrimination test on a computer, with confidence ratings. Datasets, 3D models and analysis code are openly released.
requirements: VR hardware and the custom Unreal Engine environment with distinct booths and customer characters
A recency discrimination test administered outside VR after each encoding block
constraints: Current VR environments often rely on simplified settings and artificial characters, which may limit generalizability to everyday memory processes
The salesperson task inherently emphasized customer-related goals, potentially making conceptual boundaries more salient
target_learning_goals: temporal order memory for object sequences encountered during interactive encoding
examples: Six blocks of encoding with 13 customers, 13 booths, and 25 unique objects per block, followed by desktop recency discrimination tests
key_sources: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6

article_title: Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement
citation: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6
title: Two custom first-person desktop VR learning contexts (Fairyland Garden and Moon Base) with cued mental reinstatement test protocol
description: The study built two custom, first-person desktop VR environments as learning contexts: "Fairyland Garden" was "bright, verdant, visually open", while "Moon Base" was "dark, rocky, closed-in", each containing nine named rooms. Learners navigated with mouse and keyboard, encountered 40 concrete objects per language along predetermined paths, and heard each translation three times. The contexts were created with the open source OpenSimulator platform, and a cued mental-reinstatement protocol prompted participants to imagine a specified room before each recall trial.
requirements: Measure of participants' sense of presence to confirm contexts are subjectively experienced as real environments
Control of experimenter-related cues (single audio speaker for both languages, no verbal contact during procedures)
constraints: Desktop rather than head-mounted display, which may have limited some participants' sense of presence
target_learners: Adult English speakers learning foreign vocabulary in controlled settings
target_learning_goals: Retention, transfer, and interference reduction for paired-associate foreign vocabulary learning
examples: Participants navigated Fairyland Garden and Moon Base along predetermined paths with pedestals holding objects such as a rooster labelled with its Swahili translation jogoo, tested outside VR in a laboratory, MRI scanner, and surprise telephone test

article_title: Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese?
citation: Jacqueline Żammit. (2024). Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10375-9
title: Teachers should test and experience VR first, limit student VR time, and balance VR with traditional teaching techniques
description: From the study's recommendations: teachers need to first test and experience VR before offering it to students, limit the time that VR is used by students, and be ready to answer student questions not covered by the VR application. The article states that following these recommendations makes teachers highly likely to find and maintain an optimal balance when applying VR during lessons, and that VR should be combined with traditional teaching techniques rather than replace real-life teachers.
requirements: Teacher training and continuous professional development for successful VR integration
constraints: The study's results cannot be generalized, as they depend on subjective, untested teacher comments from a small sample
target_learning_goals: Maltese as a second language proficiency
balanced technology integration in language lessons
examples: Teacher 1 stated VR cannot replace real-life teachers, but combining VR with traditional teaching techniques is a hybrid strategy that can modify the learning process

article_title: Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese?
citation: Jacqueline Żammit. (2024). Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10375-9
title: VR's immersive environment aligns with constructivist, situated, and multimodal accounts of language learning
description: The article interprets VR's potential for ML2 through several frameworks: its immersive and interactive environment aligns with the constructivist theory of learning, in which learners construct knowledge based on their experiences; real or virtual tours align with situated learning, where learning is most effective when embedded in meaningful, real-world contexts; and combining VR with traditional methods aligns with the multimodal theory of learning, which posits that different modes of communication can complement and enhance each other. Acceptance of VR is interpreted through the Technology Acceptance Model and the Theory of Diffusion of Innovations.
requirements: Further empirical investigations to clarify the practical implications of integrating VR tools into language teaching methodologies
constraints: The specific mechanisms through which VR influences language acquisition and proficiency levels are not yet fully elucidated
target_learning_goals: engagement and motivation in language learning
examples: The discussion links VR tours to situated learning and the teaching-plus-entertainment theme to edutainment and gamification concepts

article_title: Multisite usability and safety trial of an immersive virtual reality implementation of a work organization system for autistic learners: implications for technology design
citation: Herrera, G., Vera, L., Pérez-Fuster, P., López-Fernández, A., López, Á., Savaş-Taşkesen, Ü., & Newbutt, N. (2024). Multisite usability and safety trial of an immersive virtual reality implementation of a work organization system for autistic learners: implications for technology design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10422-5
title: Immersive VR implementation of the TEACCH individual work system (VR-IWS) with hand tracking and teacher customization
description: A standalone, wireless Meta Quest 2 implementation of the TEACCH individual work system comprising an input shelf, work table/area and output shelf, operated by students with their hands via hand tracking rather than controllers. Teachers configure sensory load, light-guided operation, error allowance and sessions, and can track progress. The software is "freely available in English, French, Spanish and Turkish". Four task types were implemented: moving balls, classifying objects by categories, associating objects by semantic fields, and half-and-half puzzles including simple mathematical operations.
requirements: A Meta Quest 2 HMD with hand-tracking sensors and a tablet or TV screen for streaming the participant's view to the teacher
Teacher training on the tool and on the feasibility, usability and safety measures
constraints: Tested with autistic students willing to accept and wear VR glasses at first attempt, without desensitization
Sessions limited to between 3 and 5 activities as a safety precaution
target_learners: Autistic students aged 6–17, with or without intellectual disability, in special education settings
target_learning_goals: Independent practice of acquired skills: sorting, classification, semantic association, and simple addition and subtraction
examples: In the multisite trial, teachers prepared customized sessions per student; students with lower skills performed move tasks while higher-skill students performed half-and-half puzzles involving addition and subtraction

citation: Sülter, R.E., Ketelaar, P.E., & Lange, W.G. (2022). SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children: A proof of concept. Computers & Education, 178, article 104384. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104384
title: Use VR-based speech practice as an educational tool to reduce public speaking anxiety in children.
description: This principle recommends embedding VR-based speech practice with a virtual audience into education so that children can rehearse presentations before facing a real audience. The article concludes that "this VR SpeakApp-Kids! is a promising tool to be developed further as it has potential to serve as an educational tool for speech practice and thereby reducing public speaking anxiety". It further suggests the tool can prevent public speaking anxiety from developing in the first place, making it suitable for preventive use in classrooms.
requirements: Requires access to the VR SpeakApp-Kids! application and practice sessions with a virtual audience before the actual presentation.
constraints: The article states this holds taking limitations into account, as a proof of concept rather than a fully validated intervention.
target_learning_goals: prevent public speaking anxiety from developing
examples: Children practised presentations with the SpeakApp-Kids! VR prototype across three practice sessions before delivering an actual presentation, and were compared with control children preparing at home.

article_title: Virtual reality surgical simulator training of residents and early-career surgeons for pedicle screw placement: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Pasqualotto Eric, Pasqualotto Tales, Lopes Victor Hugo Pinheiro, Lunelli Laura, Santos Lucas Loiola. (2026). Virtual reality surgical simulator training of residents and early-career surgeons for pedicle screw placement: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery & Traumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00590-026-05008-1
title: VR simulation supports surgical skill acquisition through immersive deliberate practice with immediate feedback
description: The authors' explanatory account of why VR training improves placement accuracy: VR simulators provide "an immersive, three-dimensional environment that facilitates spatial understanding of pedicle anatomy, trajectory planning, and depth perception". They add that "deliberate practice with immediate feedback allows trainees to identify errors and refine technique" without operating-room time pressure and cognitive load, and that repeated exposure in a risk-free setting may enhance procedural automation. The review invokes this account, citing prior literature, to interpret its pooled findings.
requirements: Access to a VR surgical simulator platform with sufficient fidelity to reproduce relevant anatomy and procedural workflows
constraints: The account is an authors' interpretation supported by cited background literature, not a mechanism tested within the review itself
examples: The review's six RCTs trained participants on simulators including ImmersiveSimTM, VSTS and IVRSS-PSP for 30–40 minutes per session before assessing placement accuracy on sawbone, cadaveric specimens or patients

article_title: Virtual reality simulation to teach communication for undergraduate nursing students: a scoping review.
citation: Deng Jing, Tan Yifei, Chen Jing, Guo Xiujing, Wang Ling, Xie Chuan. (2025). Virtual reality simulation to teach communication for undergraduate nursing students: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08450-7
title: VR simulation as a pedagogical platform for communication skills training in undergraduate nursing education
description: The review organizes evidence on VR simulation for communication training around VR's core characteristics: "interaction, immersion, immediacy, participation, and presence". These enable high-fidelity, clinically relevant communication environments that provide a safe platform for practice with flexible scheduling and customizable learning experiences. The framework positions VR as enabling safe, private practice of high-risk scenarios and deliberate, repeated practice using standardized, on-demand scenarios, supporting simulation-based mastery learning and deliberate practice frameworks.
requirements: VR simulation systems require explicit documentation of implementation methodology and validated assessment instruments for communication skills
constraints: The review notes a demonstrable gap between technological capabilities and human performance, particularly in replicating complex therapeutic communication within clinical contexts
examples: The seven included studies used virtual patients, AI doctor agents, and 3D immersive scenarios built in the Unity 3D game engine for communication practice

title: Use virtual reality simulation prior to performing real cataract surgery cases
description: The review concludes that virtual reality simulation appears to lead to safer outcomes than supervised surgical training on actual patients alone, "which encourages its use prior to performing real cases". Simulators enable repeated training on surgical steps without risking patient injury, and a VRS phase before surgery on actual patients, as in the HMS curriculum, may help reduce complication rates.

constraints: Virtual reality simulators are sparsely distributed around the world with numerous access difficulties and lack of standardization between training programs
target_learners: Ophthalmology residents and trainees who have not yet completed specialty training
target_learning_goals: Safe cataract surgery performance in the operating room
examples: The review cites the HMS training curriculum and one EyeSi study that proposed a VRS phase prior to surgery on actual patients

Virtual reality simulation in robot-assisted surgery: meta-analysis of skill transfer and predictability of skill. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zraa066
title: Use robotic VR simulator training before operating on patients, as acquired skills transfer to the operating room
description: The review concludes that "Technical surgical skills acquired through robotic VR simulator training can be transferred to the operating room", so that "VR training can therefore be justified before operating on patients". The authors argue this supports including robotic VR simulators in dedicated training curricula and emphasizes simulation training before real operating room performance to ensure patient safety. Shortened operating times further justify simulators because operating room time is expensive.

target_learners: novice robotic surgeons, surgical residents, and credentialed surgeons naive to robot-assisted surgery
target_learning_goals: technical robotic surgical skill acquisition and transfer to operating room performance
examples: In the reviewed studies, intervention groups trained on dVSS or dV-Trainer tasks to proficiency before operating room assessment on human patients or live animal models

article_title: Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines
citation: Zheng Wei, Junxiang Liao, Lik-Hang Lee, Huamin Qu, and Xian Xu. (2025). Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13845
title: Five-type presence taxonomy for VR learning environments: spatial, social, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence
description: The review organizes VR presence research around five presence types identified across the included studies: spatial presence, social presence, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence. The abstract states the review provides "a detailed classification and analysis of different types of presence in VR environments, including spatial presence, social presence, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence." Each type is defined by its function: spatial presence concerns perceiving position and spatial relationships, cognitive presence concerns deep thinking and knowledge construction, social presence concerns interaction quality, co-presence concerns shared awareness, and self-presence concerns identity and embodiment. The taxonomy structures the review's data extraction (DE4), its mapping of presence types to task functions, and its design recommendations.
requirements: Studies must manipulate or measure at least one of the five presence types to be classifiable within this framework
constraints: Derived from 78 studies published 2020-2024 in VR education and collaboration contexts
target_learners: VR learners across education, engineering, and collaborative training contexts
examples: The review's data extraction rubric (DE4) codes each of the 78 included studies by which of the five presence types it addresses
key_sources: Zheng Wei, Junxiang Liao, Lik-Hang Lee, Huamin Qu, and Xian Xu. (2025). Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13845

description: A unique screen-based VR program, built for desktop use, that visualizes the bony landmarks of the anterior thoracic wall and lets learners place six precordial and two upper limb ECG leads on a virtual patient lying on a hospital bed. title: VR simulation design combining 3D anatomical visualization, immediate error feedback, and repeatable practice

title: Vroom's expectancy theory: valence, instrumentality, expectancy, and the valence and force models
description: Expectancy theory holds that motivation arises from a conscious, rational weighing of behavioral alternatives using three constructs: expectancy (the probability that effort leads to a goal), instrumentality (how essential goal attainment is for second-level outcomes), and valence (anticipated satisfaction with those outcomes). article_title: Development of simulated arthroscopic skills.
citation: Andersen C, Winding TN, Vesterby MS. (2011). Development of simulated arthroscopic skills: A randomized trial of virtual-reality training of 21 orthopedic surgeons. Acta Orthopaedica 82(1). https://doi.org/10.3109/17453674.2011.552776
title: Use short immersive VR simulator training programs to help inexperienced surgeons acquire basic navigation skills before supervised real surgery
description: The article supports offering novice surgeons structured virtual-reality simulator training before they perform arthroscopy in the operating theater, where time pressure and patient safety limit learning opportunities. A 5-hour training program on the VR unit, starting with advice on basic navigation skills from a more experienced surgeon and then systematic practice of the simulator's tests, produced marked improvement: "VR training is a possible way for young and inexperienced surgeons to achieve basic navigation skills necessary to perform arthroscopic surgery." The authors caution that transfer of these skills to actual surgery remains to be demonstrated.
requirements: A validated VR arthroscopic trainer with automatically recorded performance parameters, an instructor available for guidance, and control groups kept from using the unit during the intervening period
constraints: The authors state further studies on transferability of VR-acquired skills to the operating theater are desirable, and that the small sample size provided statistical uncertainty
target_learners: young and inexperienced surgeons and orthopedic interns
target_learning_goals: basic arthroscopic navigation skills, efficient instrument movement, and reduced tissue damage during arthroscopy
examples: 7 interns with no arthroscopic experience completed a 5-hour VR training program and were retested approximately 1 week later, improving on all 5 evaluated parameters relative to untrained controls
